newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore "surprised" Malaysia says ties need time.
newsitem.headline: Singapore "surprised" Malaysia says ties need time.

text.p: Singapore has expressed surprised at a statement by Malaysia that the relationship between the two neighbours, rocked by comments from Singapore Senior Minister Lee Kuan Yew, would take time to heal.

"The government of Singapore is surprised that the Malaysian government has stated that 'restoration of the old level of relationship would take time'," Singapore Foreign Affairs Minister Shanmugam Jayakumar said in a statement released late on Wednesday.

Malaysian Foreign Minister Abdullah Badawi told reporters on Wednesday Kuala Lumpur accepted Lee's apology for describing the south Malaysian state of Johor as "notorious for shootings, muggings and car-jackings" in a Singapore court affidavit.
Abdullah said after a cabinet meeting that Malaysia also viewed positively Lee's move to get the offending remarks deleted from the affidavit.
But he said: "However, it should be acknowledged that this episode has deeply hurt Malaysians of all sections of society and that restoration of the old level of relationship would take time."

Jayakumar's statement noted Malaysia had accepted Lee's apology. It stressed that the comments by Lee, Singapore's prime minister from 1959 to 1990, were made by him personally and when he was acting in a private capacity.
"The affidavit was not made by (Lee) as senior minister, nor did he make it on behalf of the government of Singapore," Jayakumar said.
"The government of Singapore has always attached importance to its relations with Malaysia and will work with the Malaysian government to enhance this relationship," he said.
"We believe that cooperation between the two countries can only result in a win-win situation," he said.
Lee's comments sparked one of the worst diplomatic rows in years between the two nations, with Malaysia demanding an apology and retraction.

Malaysia is a key trading partner of Singapore and also supplies much of its water, food and raw materials. But the two countries are also fierce competitors for regional economic power and influence.

The comments on Johor became front page news in Malaysia after the affidavit, filed on January 27 as part of a libel suit against Singapore opposition politician Tang Liang Hong, was leaked to the media.
Tang fled to Johor Baru, the capital of Johor state, after losing a race for parliament in the January 2 general elections. He later said he left Singapore because he feared for his life.
Lee, however, questioned Tang's decision for choosing Johor, saying "that place is notorious for shootings, muggings and car-jackings".
Following the furore caused in Malaysia by his statement, the 73-year-old elder statesman issued a statement through his office apologising "unreservedly" for his remarks on Johor.
But Malaysians remained enraged, demanding he retract the remarks. The youth wing of Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's party even threatened to sue.
Lee repeated his apology in a signed statement on Tuesday, and said he had instructed his lawyer to ask the court's permission to have the remarks on Johor deleted.
